extracted.intended_audience: H-1B petitioning employers, immigration stakeholders, commenters, and legal/policy practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Extraction of rulemaking criteria and standards used in the DHS Federal Register preamble justifying and explaining a weighted H-1B selection process that prioritizes higher-paid and higher-skilled beneficiaries while responding to public comments. Focuses on how weighting is calculated, expected impacts, and policy objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary rule objective: favor allocation to higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens
rubrics_metrics.description: "The goal of this rule is to favor the allocation of H-1B visas to higher-skilled and higher-paid aliens."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS states the weighted selection process will generally favor allocation to higher-skilled, higher-paid aliens, facilitate admission of higher-skilled workers, benefit the economy, increase U.S. competitiveness, and align with the H-1B program goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentive effect: weight to encourage employers to proffer higher wages or higher-skilled positions
rubrics_metrics.description: The weighted selection process is intended to "incentivize all H-1B cap-subject employers ... to offer higher wages to increase their chances of selection, thereby aligning with the program’s goal of prioritizing highly skilled and highly paid workers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS repeatedly invokes this as the mechanism to reduce reliance on lower-paid, lower-skilled filings and to protect U.S. workers' wages and opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighted selection mechanics: use highest equivalent wage level tied to proffered salary
rubrics_metrics.description: The weighting process is "generally based on the highest wage level that the proffered salary would equal or exceed and is not based purely on Department of Labor (DOL) wage levels."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For registration purposes the proffered salary is considered; the OEWS wage-level framework is relevant only if OEWS wage data is not available. A position classified as level I for LCA purposes can be assigned a higher equivalent wage level for weighting if the proffered salary justifies it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not change statutory numerical caps
rubrics_metrics.description: This rule "does not restrict the number of H-1B visas available under the statutory cap" and "does not alter the numerical limitations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS emphasizes the rule only changes the selection mechanism in years of excess demand, not the total number of cap-subject visas available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain access across all wage levels
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS recognizes "the value in maintaining the opportunity for employers to secure H-1B workers at all wage levels."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule differs from prior approaches (e.g., 2021 ranking rule) by preserving a non-zero selection chance for level I and II positions; DHS projects specific selection probabilities (see Table 13) to demonstrate retained access.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neutrality across company types and industries
rubrics_metrics.description: The weighted registration process "is not intended to treat any companies or industries better or worse than others."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS asserts the objective is to favor higher-paid, higher-skilled aliens regardless of employer type (including large tech, outsourcers, startups, H-1B-dependent employers), and that the rule should not be interpreted as intentionally advantaging particular firms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect wages, working conditions, and job opportunities of U.S. workers
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule should "better protect the wages, working conditions, and job opportunities of U.S. workers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS frames the weighted selection as a tool to reduce program abuse that depresses wages and displaces U.S. workers; incentives to proffer higher wages are presented as protective of the domestic labor market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require evidence for asserted negative economic impacts
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS repeatedly notes commenters "did not provide data" and that analyses lacking appropriate evidence are not persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims that the rule will harm the economy or specific industries, DHS expects commenters to provide robust supporting data; absent such evidence, DHS deems many assertions overstated or unsubstantiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider cap-exempt occupations and alternative immigration pathways
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain occupations (e.g., professors and doctors) "are usually cap-exempt or have other immigration pathways" and thus "would likely have little effect."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Impact assessments should account for occupations with cap exemptions or alternative programs (J-1, Conrad 30, etc.) when estimating practical effects on national sectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: H-1B program purpose: fill shortages in highly skilled/highly educated positions
rubrics_metrics.description: The H-1B program was created to "help U.S. employers fill labor shortages in positions requiring highly skilled or highly educated workers while protecting the wages, working conditions, and job opportunities of U.S. workers."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy decisions and assessments should be framed by this stated statutory/program purpose, distinguishing appropriate H-1B uses from alleged program abuse (replacement of U.S. workers with lower-paid labor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule does not affect OPT or prevent F-1 to H-1B transitions
rubrics_metrics.description: "This rule has no impact on OPT." DHS states it "will not preclude F-1 students ... from transitioning from OPT to employment under the H-1B visa or 'force' such students to leave."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS notes that F-1 graduates offered higher wages may be advantaged under the weighting; the rule preserves the opportunity for transitions even if lower-paid offers have reduced selection probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of projected selection probabilities as evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS cites projected probabilities (e.g., "level I ... 15.29-percent probability", "level II ... 30.58%") and references NPRM Table 13 as a measure of expected outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These projections are offered to compare the weighted process against the prior random selection approach and to show that level II/III probabilities increase while level I decreases but remains non-zero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not conflate DOL Wage Levels with actual pay or merit
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS acknowledges that "DOL’s Wage Levels are very different from actual wages" and that wage levels measure relative seniority within an occupation, not absolute pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The weighting accounts for the proffered salary (actual pay) and not solely the OEWS wage-level classification; commenters' critiques that rely only on DOL wage-level semantics may misunderstand the rule's mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallback: use OEWS wage-level data only when proffered salary/OEWS unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: For registration purposes, the requirements corresponding to the DOL wage level "would only be relevant if OEWS wage data is not available."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a procedural rule for determining equivalent wage levels when occupancy-specific OEWS data cannot be matched.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address program abuse where H-1B replaces rather than supplements U.S. workers
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule targets "the specific problem ... the abuse of the H-1B program to bring in lower-skilled workers in lower-paid positions."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: DHS frames the weighted selection as a corrective measure to reverse large-scale replacement of U.S. workers and to strengthen economic and national security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyses of distributional effects must account for multiple registrations and firm heterogeneity
rubrics_metrics.description: DHS criticizes analyses that group firms (e.g., firms registering >2,000 H-1Bs) as outsourcers without accounting for multiple registrations per beneficiary and other factors, concluding such analyses "are not persuasive."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robust empirical claims about who benefits or loses under the rule should control for multiple eligible registrations per beneficiary, firm-level heterogeneity, and correct interpretation of the weighting mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule does not mandate employer wages; assumes economic rationality
rubrics_metrics.description: "This rule does not mandate what wages employers must pay their employees" and DHS expects "rational employers will not offer wages exceeding the expected value of the employee’s work."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory design relies on employer economic decisions: employers may offer higher wages only when it is in their economic interest rather than being compelled to overpay.
